functions, variables
docs.text:
in python, you dont need to declare variables

input and print are the frequent ones for now.

you can print a string by just using print(name) here. so much easier

print has a implicit end='\n' argument. you can change it by expliciting said argument and putting whatever you want there there's also sep=", ") to separate itens if you're printing a list or smth

use \" if you need quotations in a string and is too lazy to change the function ones for single ones.

put an f at the start of a string if you want to use variables with {} inside of her. example:

smth = "example"
print(f"this is a {smth}")

btw you can multiply prints. yeah.

docs.title: more in strings
docs.text:
use .method to apply that method to a string you can stack multiple methods

strip() to remove spaces on both sides of str title() title cases the words lower() makes it all lower case

official str documentation: https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str

docs.title: integers and float
docs.text:
the operators are pretty similar to c except you dont have i++

use float() or int() to convert

round(n,[digit])is self explanatory

you can also use that f thingy from str print(f"{z:.2f}")

official documentations: https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float

docs.title: def
docs.text:
this is what you use to create your own functions. an example i like, idk why

def hello(to):
    print("hello,", to)

name = input("What's your name? ")
hello(name)

return can pass manyyyyyyy values. numbers, lists, tumbles, dictionaries... many many stuff.

docs.title: conditionals
docs.text:
not much to say. just probably the most pythonic part of python

match can be used to improve readbility. example:

from: 

  name = input("What's your name? ")

  if name == "Harry" or name == "Hermione" or name == "Ron": 
      print("Gryffindor")
  elif name == "Draco":
      print("Slytherin")
  else:
      print("Who?")

to: 

  name = input("What's your name? ")

  match name: 
      case "Harry" | "Hermione" | "Ron":
          print("Gryffindor")
      case "Draco":
          print("Slytherin")
      case _:
          print("Who?")

yes you can use both symbols and just plain english. python moment

official documentation: https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html

docs.title: loops
docs.text:
for in python is pretty weird. it does all the job for you.

like if you want to run 3 times just do for i in range(3). the control variable is created and manipulated automatically.

you can also provide a list such as for i in [0,1,2] to be traversed if u want to

you can use _ in place of i. and any variable that serves no purpose other than loop iteration

break out of the loop! continue next iteration

if you have any kind of data structure (more about that soon) you can use this formatting: for thing in structure

it will instantly know to follow the list.

str are included in data structures in this case (cuz its an char list lowkey)

docs.title: lists
docs.text:
various values.

you can make a list and access it like an C array. 

example = ["one", "two", "three"]

print(example[0])
# one
print(example[1])
# two
print(example[2])
# three

use len to see how many items the list contains.

official documentation: https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#len https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#more-on-lists

docs.title: dictionaries
docs.text:
basically a list but you can assign value to each item and access it. its basically keys with a value.

students = {
    "Hermione": "Gryffindor",
}
print(students["Hermione"])
# Gryffindor

you can make a list of multiple dictionaries!!

official documentation: https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#dictionaries

docs.title: notes
docs.text:
~ is an alias for home directory

compiled program ; coded on human versions of machine code, run natively in your pc by using a compiler. due to that, it's pretty fast. low portability. examples are Go, C and Rust interpreted program ; executed by another program first, needs the interpreter. slower cuz it translates then executes every line. high portability. examples are Python, Ruby and JS

easy analogy: compiler is like translating a book and you read it. interpreter is like someone reading each sentence in their language, then translating it to you.

shebang: line at the top of a script that tells your shell which program to use. format: interpreter [optional-arg]

docs.title: shell
docs.text:
the program that reads your commands. aka REPLs

i actually use fish but the notes here will be on bash

there's also zsh but i haven't touched it

an sh which bash was based on

they're all POSIX-compliant except for fish (sort of)

docs.title: commands
docs.text:
you can run multiple commands by separating then with a semicolon ; if you want the second only if the first succeed, &&

pwd printing current working directory /home absolute path cd moving around mkdir create directory mv move and rename stuff echo shell says what u ask

cp copy stuff. flags: -r rm permanently remove files. flags: -r, -f force.

ls listing the contents of a directory. flags: -a, -r, -i inode, -l all info, t descending order, -S sort by size, -X alphabetical, -1 one file per line

cat concatenate. see the contents of files head see the start. flags: -n number of lines tail see the end. flags: same

less paging through a file. commands: space down one page. b up one page. / search. q quit. more worse version of less

touch useful to create empty files only when non existent

grep search for text in files, case sensitively. flags: -r paired with . on path find finding stuff by name. be it title or pattern (such as filetype)

i always mix up the syntax of those two

grep "example" file.txt
find directory -name "example"

which location of an installed CLI program, such as shell

docs.title: variables
docs.text:
use $ to access variables.

PATH built-in variable on how to execute stuff. check its own section

env to see all environment variables currently set

$HOME self explanatory $? exit code of the last program you ran

export set a variable for this session only unset remove a variable for this session only

docs.title: flags and arguments
docs.text:
usually - for letter and -- for words.

-h or --help is self explanatory

you can combine flags.

often a command take multiple arguments, one of them possibly being a flag. the syntax is usually intuitive.

docs.title: path
docs.text:
$PATH is the variable that guards a list of directions that your shell will look into when you try to run a command.

they probably contain /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin but you can add whatever.

remember to add $PATH itself in order to not overwrite the existing path. 

reminder that the shell runs on RAM so it won't be a permanent change. you'd have to add into your initialization file to get it on every session.

docs.title: imput and output
docs.text:
$? check the exit code of the last program you ran.

stdout output. yeah. redirect it with > stderr like stdout but for error messages. redirect it with 2> stdin input. shocking. redirect it with <

piping: taking the output of a program directly into the input of another program. very useful for automation tasks.

| is the pipe operator.

docs.title: DNS (Domain Name System)
docs.text: DNS translates domain names into IP addresses, allowing devices to locate services on a network.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
When a user accesses example.com, the resolver looks up the corresponding IP address.

A simplified lookup process:

  1. Check the local DNS cache.
  2. Query a recursive resolver.
  3. If necessary, query the root DNS server.
  4. Locate the authoritative nameserver.
  5. Return the IP address.

docs.title: Common record types
docs.text: Record Purpose A Maps a domain to an IPv4 address AAAA Maps a domain to an IPv6 address CNAME Creates an alias for another domain MX Specifies mail servers NS Identifies authoritative nameservers TXT Stores text-based information

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
Check the IP address associated with a domain:

dig example.com

Query a specific record:

dig example.com A

Check the nameservers:

dig example.com NS

Alternative:

nslookup example.com

docs.title: Important ports
docs.text:
Protocol Port DNS (UDP) 53 DNS (TCP) 53

Remember

DNS usually uses UDP port 53, but TCP is also used in specific situations, such as zone transfers and responses requiring TCP.

docs.title: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol)
docs.text: HTTP is an application-layer protocol used for communication between clients and servers.

docs.title: Request and response
docs.text:
An HTTP communication typically consists of:

  1. A client sends a request.
  2. The server processes it.
  3. The server returns a response.

docs.title: HTTP methods
docs.text: Method Description GET Retrieve a resource POST Submit data PUT Replace a resource PATCH Partially modify a resource DELETE Remove a resource HEAD Retrieve headers without the response body

docs.title: Status codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 200 OK 201 Created 301 Moved Permanently 400 Bad Request 401 Unauthorized 403 Forbidden 404 Not Found 500 Internal Server Error 503 Service Unavailable

docs.title: Example request
docs.text:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Accept: text/html

Example response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
Make a GET request:

curl https://example.com

Display response headers:

curl -I https://example.com

docs.title: HTTP vs HTTPS
docs.text:
• HTTP transmits application data without transport encryption.
  • HTTPS uses TLS to protect communication between client and server.

Remember

HTTPS normally uses TCP port 443, while HTTP traditionally uses TCP port 80.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• RFC 9110 — HTTP Semantics
  • MDN — HTTP

docs.title: What is a computer network?
docs.text:
A computer network is a collection of interconnected devices that communicate and exchange data using agreed-upon rules called protocols.

Examples of networked devices include computers, smartphones, servers, routers, and switches.

docs.title: Why does networking matter?
docs.text:
Networking enables devices and applications to communicate locally and across the internet.

It is fundamental to:

  • Web applications and APIs
  • Cloud computing
  • Distributed systems
  • Infrastructure and Site Reliability Engineering (SRE)
  • Network security and troubleshooting

docs.title: changing the title
docs.text:
by default, fastfetch utilizes the module title to show the users name and the machines hostname. however, im too lazy to migrate my user to the one i actually like, so i just put a mask on everything to hide it.

just add a format section and put whatever you want there.

{
    "type": "title",
    "format": "user@hostname"
}

docs.title: changing colors
docs.text:
example: purple and cyan.

{
    "type": "title",
    "format": "{#magenta}scythe{#}@{#cyan}my-system{#}"
}
  • {#color}: self explanatory
  • {#}: back to original color
